fact_en: Bigger filter holes let water flow faster, but more dirt slips through! Fine holes filter slower but give cleaner water. It's a trade-off between speed and cleanliness!
fact_bis: Mas dagkong lungag sa filter mas paspas, pero mas daghang hugaw ang makalusot! Ang fine holes mas hinay pero mas limpyo. Baylohanay kini sa katulin ug kalimpyo!

findings.note: Title garbled and wrong-thing: title_en "Big Holes Fast Dirty" -> "Daku nga Lung Mabilis Baho" — "Lung" is a truncated lungag, and Baho = odour, so the headline reads "big hole, fast smell" instead of anything about dirt slipping through.

fact_en: Most diamonds are billions of years old — they're older than almost every living thing on Earth!
fact_bis: Kadaghanan sa diamante minilyon ka tuig na — mas tigulang pa kini kaysa halos tanan buhing butang sa Yuta!

findings.note: Number changed by 1000x: en "Most diamonds are billions of years old" but bis says "Kadaghanan sa diamante minilyon ka tuig na" = millions of years. The body is the only sentence stating the age, so a child reads the wrong magnitude (and it even contradicts the card's own title "Bilyon Tuig Diamante").

fact_en:
Why does bread turn brown in a toaster?

It is a chemical reaction between sugars and proteins! The new brown layer and the tasty smell are both signs that this yummy reaction happened.
fact_bis:
Ngano mahimong kapehon ang tinapay sa toaster?

Reaksiyong kemikal kana tali sa kalamian ug protina! Ang bag-ong kapehon nga bahin ug lami nga baho parehong timailhan sa reaksiyon.

findings.note: Core reactant lost: en "a chemical reaction between sugars and proteins" becomes "Reaksiyong kemikal kana tali sa kalamian ug protina" — kalami/kalamian is DELICIOUSNESS/flavour in Cebuano, not sugar (asukal). The card never says asukal anywhere, so a child ends up believing browning is a reaction between "flavour" and protein.

fact_en: Besides carbon dioxide, rice farms and animals like cattle and water buffalo release methane, another strong greenhouse gas. With our many rice fields, this also warms our world!
fact_bis: Gawas sa carbon dioxide, ang mga humayan ug hayop sama sa baka ug kabaw mobuga ug methane, lain nga kusgan nga greenhouse gas. Tungod sa daghang humayan, makapainit usab kini sa kalibotan!

findings.note: title_bis "Methane Uma Bakawan" — English title is "Rice Animals Methane". "Bakawan" is MANGROVE (a mangrove swamp/forest), not animals; it looks like a garbled squeeze of "baka ug kabaw". The headline therefore names a different methane source (mangroves) than the card, and the body never mentions mangroves at all, so nothing in the Cebuano corrects it — a child scanning the title is left believing mangroves are the methane source. Body itself is correct ("humayan ug hayop sama sa baka ug kabaw"), so the fix is title-only: e.g. "Methane Uma, Baka ug Kabaw".

fact_en:
Why put baking soda or vinegar on an ant or bee sting?

Some stings are acidic, so a mild base like baking soda can neutralize them for relief. But always ask a doctor first, since not all stings are the same!
fact_bis:
Ngano butangan og baking soda o suka ang paak sa langgam o buyog?

Ang uban nga paak kay acidic, busa ang baking soda makahimo og neutralize ug makahatag og kahupayan. Apan mangutana una sa doktor, kay dili tanan nga paak parehas!

findings.note: Body: "Ngano butangan og baking soda o suka ang paak sa langgam o buyog?" — English is "an ant or bee sting", but langgam is BIRD in Cebuano (ant = hulmigas/subay). The card never says ant anywhere else, so a Cebuano-only reader learns to treat a BIRD bite with baking soda. Title ("Pangtambal sa Paak") is generic and does not restore the animal.

fact_en: Iron is solid and strong, so we make hammers, bolos, and nails from it! It doesn't bend easily, meaning your tools last a long time.
fact_bis: Solid ug lig-on ang puthaw, mao nga gihimo kining martilyo, sundang, ug lansang! Dili dali mobaliko, mao nga dugay magamit ang imong kasangkapan.

findings.note: title_bis "Iron Martilyo Itak Pako" for EN "Iron Solid Tools". Cebuano pako = WING (nail = lansang, used correctly in the body); itak is also Tagalog for bolo (Cebuano sundang). The title lists iron tools as "hammer, bolo, wing".

fact_en:
Is it safe to play with flowing liquid mercury?

No, it is poisonous! Even if the silvery metal looks cool, never touch it. Tell an adult right away if a thermometer breaks.
fact_bis:
Luwas ba nga magdula sa nagdagayday nga likidong mercury?

Dili, makahilo kini! Bisan mukhang cool ang pilak nga metal, ayaw hikapa. Sultihi dayon ang adult kung adunay nabuak nga termometro.

findings.note: title_bis "Mercury Hilo Dili Hawak" for EN "Mercury Not a Toy". Cebuano hawak = WAIST; the Tagalog sense (to hold) is not available in Cebuano (hold = gunit/kupot; body uses hikap). The safety headline becomes "Mercury poison not waist".

fact_en:
Ever wonder why you float better after a big breath?

When you breathe in deeply, your lungs fill with air! This makes you lighter and helps you float on your back in the water.
fact_bis:
Ngano nga mas sayon molutaw pagkahuman sa lawom nga ginhawa?

Kung lawom ang imong ginhawa, mapuno sa hangin ang imong baga! Mao nga mas gaan ka ug mas sayon molutaw nga naghapa sa tubig.

findings.note: Body reverses body position: EN 'helps you float on your back in the water' -> BIS 'mas sayon molutaw nga naghapa sa tubig'. In Cebuano naghapa = lying FACE-DOWN (prone); on your back is naghayang. Nothing in the card corrects it, so a child who reads only the Cebuano is told the deep-breath trick lets you float face-down - the drowning position - rather than on your back. Direction reversed + safety-relevant.

fact_en: Pewter is a soft alloy mostly made of tin. It's easy to shape, so it's used for plates, cups, and pretty decorations!
fact_bis: Ang pewter usa ka malambot nga alloy nga gihimo sa tin. Sayon kini hubogon, busa gigamit sa mga plato, tasa, ug mga nindot nga dekorasyon!

findings.note: "Sayon kini hubogon" for "It's easy to shape" — hubog is Tagalog for shape/mold but in Cebuano means DRUNK, so the clause reads "it is easy to get drunk" and the reason pewter is used for plates/cups (its malleability) is dropped with no restoration elsewhere in the card. Cebuano would be "sayon hulmahon/pormahon".

fact_en: The carbon in steel controls its hardness! High-carbon steel is hard but brittle, while low-carbon steel is softer and easier to shape.
fact_bis: Ang carbon sa steel ang nagkontrol sa katig-a! Ang high-carbon steel matigas apan madaling mabuto, samtang ang low-carbon steel mas malambot ug mas sayon hubogon.

findings.note: "Ang high-carbon steel matigas apan madaling mabuto" — Cebuano buto = explode/burst, so the card states high-carbon steel EXPLODES easily, not that it is brittle/snaps (cf. ffct-17882, same topic, correctly says "dali mabali sama sa tisa"). Nothing in the card corrects it, so the child learns a false property. The same sentence also has the Tagalog false friend "mas sayon hubogon" — Cebuano hubog = DRUNK (shape/mold = hulma; ffct-17886 correctly uses "hulmahon"), so "easier to shape" is lost too.

fact_en:
How does smoking fish like tinapa keep it from spoiling?

Smoke contains special chemicals called phenols that slow down bacterial growth, keeping the fish fresh and tasty for longer!
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagpreserba sa isda sama sa tinapa pinaagi sa panisigarilyo?

Ang aso adunay mga kemikal nga phenols nga nagpugong sa pagtubo sa bacteria, mao nga mas dugay nga presko ug lami ang isda!

findings.note: EN asks how smoking fish like tinapa preserves it. The Cebuano question reads 'Unsaon pagpreserba sa isda sama sa tinapa pinaagi sa panisigarilyo?' — panisigarilyo means CIGARETTE-smoking, a different thing entirely. Nothing in the card corrects the source of the smoke: the answer only says 'Ang aso adunay mga kemikal nga phenols', which is equally true of cigarette smoke, so it reinforces rather than repairs. A child is left believing tinapa is preserved by smoking cigarettes at the fish. Verified against the rest of the corpus: every other food-smoking card uses pag-aso / pagpaaso / pinausukan (ffct-20725, ffct-15748, ffct-19053, ffct-05878, ffct-15773 ...); 'panisigarilyo' occurs exactly once corpus-wide, here. Fix: 'pinaagi sa pagpaaso'.

fact_en: Natural fibers like cotton and abaca are biodegradable and break down in nature! But synthetic fibers like polyester don't break down easily and last for hundreds of years.
fact_bis: Ang natural fibers sama sa cotton ug abaca biodegradable ug madunot sa kinaiyahan! Pero ang synthetic fibers sama sa polyester dili dali madunot ug magpabilin sulod sa daan-tuig.

findings.note: EN: synthetic fibers like polyester 'last for hundreds of years'. BIS: 'magpabilin sulod sa daan-tuig'. 'Daan' is the TAGALOG word for hundred (isang daan); in Cebuano daan means OLD/former, so 'daan-tuig' reads as 'old years' and the quantity is gone — the card's punchline contrast (biodegradable vs. persists for centuries) cannot be answered from the Cebuano, and nothing else in this card states a duration. Corpus check confirms this is a defect, not house style: 'gatusan ka tuig' appears 31 times corpus-wide, 'daan(-/ ka )tuig' only twice — both in this batch. The other instance, ffct-17979 ('sulod sa daan ka tuig'), I PASSED because the same card restores it with 'sa hataas kaayong panahon', but it should be fixed together with this one.
